source.title: Investigating Generalization by Controlling Normalized Margin
source.authors: Alexander R. Farhang; Jeremy Bernstein; Kushal Tirumala; Yang Liu; Yisong Yue

record.tranche_reason: The study controls normalized-margin distributions and reports effects on test performance, a conceptual test of generalization alongside label memorization.
record.gate_note: The study reports true-label and random-label MNIST results relevant to V1. Its normalized-margin results concern a different measure from V7's magnitude-aware sharpness; those findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited prior results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V1 in a new MNIST setting: identical MLP architectures fit natural and fixed random labels, with above-chance natural-label test accuracy and approximately chance random-label test accuracy. Its main normalized-margin experiments address a different claim from V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: normalized margin is insufficient to explain generalization universally, but controlling it can control test performance in less adversarial settings. The proposed Gaussian-process model also predicts the observed similarity between increasing normalized margin and averaging more ensemble members.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled margin targeting, label scaling, input normalization, and projected gradient methods to investigate margin's causal relationship with generalization; V1's named benchmark setups are not reproduced.
record.method_sensitivity: The relationship between normalized margin and generalization changes with the control setting: spectrally normalized margin tracks generalization in one setup but reverses in another; true-label test performance varies with targeted normalized margin in standard training.

fits_no_version.finding: Controlled optimization reverses the ordering of spectrally normalized margins between generalizing and non-generalizing networks; matched Frobenius-normalized margins can accompany different test accuracies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized-margin distributions alone are insufficient to explain generalization across the tested controlled settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In standard MNIST training, larger targeted normalized margins tend to improve test accuracy; increasing ensemble size produces similar improvements in finite networks and Gaussian-process draws.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted normalized margin and ensemble size control test performance in the tested MNIST settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Sampled and gradient-trained twins can have different test accuracy despite nearly identical training outputs and normalized margins across several widths and binary classification tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization procedure can affect generalization beyond what matched normalized margins explain.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 162, 2022
record.problems: The paper's Figure 1 description reports 81% test accuracy for the correctly labeled network, while Appendix A.1 reports 88% for the corresponding network. Figure-based margin distributions and several margin-versus-accuracy curves do not provide exact values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numeric result rows were needed for V1. The controlled normalized-margin findings in Sections 4.1, 4.2, and 5.1 are not mapped to V7 because the study does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness; the supplied text gives several of those findings as figure descriptions without exact values.

untested.parts: The original CIFAR-10 and ImageNet architectures and datasets are not reproduced. Identical hyperparameters across label conditions are not tested because target scales differ. The Nero comparison does not test coexistence without explicit weight constraints, and the unconstrained comparison stops at approximately 95% training accuracy rather than perfect fit.
The width sweeps compare sampled and trained twins; they do not establish continued improvement beyond a measured zero-training-error width threshold under the specified training conditions.
No adaptive-versus-SGD comparison under a defined tuning budget.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
Neither magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness nor its ranking of generalization gaps against competing measures is evaluated.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence and comparison with random removal.

missing.what: Figure 10 reports additional paired natural- and random-label training/test accuracy curves across targeted normalized margins. These bear on V1 and are not specifically accounted for in rows_left_out. The supplied text does not preserve enough curve geometry to assign numerical values or condition-specific verdicts.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V1. Different target scales and explicit Nero constraints qualify what was tested; they do not themselves demonstrate failure of V1. The margin counterexamples do not challenge V7's distinct correlational sharpness claim.

versions.untested_parts: The specified Inception, AlexNet, and MLP benchmarks and the named Zhang et al. settings were not tested; the study reports its own MNIST experiments.
The study controls normalized margins, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
